Two minutes, and I will spend the first thirty seconds on what has not gone well, because it is the part you will remember anyway. We said we would close the engineering pipeline gap this year and we have not. It is exactly where it was in January, and I have run out of explanations that are not just the same explanation. Granted, we lost the two people who were building it. That is true and it does not solve anything. What has worked is the first ninety days. Attrition under one year of service has come down eleven points since March, whereas attrition over three years has not moved, which is what we expected and what we wanted. By and large the onboarding redesign has done what we said it would do. Having said that, it has done it in three sites out of five, and the two that are missing are the two that need it most. All things considered, I would rather have this problem than the one we had in January.

She did the thing almost nobody does, which is start with the failure. And I want to be precise about why that works on me, because it is not about honesty and it is not about humility. It is about arithmetic. If somebody spends two minutes on the good news, I have to spend the rest of the meeting working out what they left out, and I am not a generous auditor. If they hand me the bad one in the first thirty seconds, I believe the rest, and we get to spend the time on the decision instead of on the search. The second thing she did was concede one point and refuse to let it do more work than it deserved. Granted, we lost two people. That is true and it does not solve anything. I have watched people spend four minutes on an excuse that good. And the third one, honestly, is that she stopped talking at two minutes. I asked three questions and every one of them was about what to do next. That is a good meeting.
